question_text: The region of space around a charged body where another charged body will experience an electric force is called:
explanation: An electric field is the region of space around a charged body where another charged body will experience an electric force. It is created by source charges and its SI unit is Newton per Coulomb (N/C).

question_text: The electric field vector \(\vec{E}\) at a point is defined as:
explanation: The electric field \(\vec{E}\) at a point is the electric force \(\vec{F}\) experienced by a small positive test charge \(q_0\) placed at that point, divided by the magnitude of that charge: \(\vec{E} = \vec{F}/q_0\).

options.text: The total charge at the point divided by the distance squared
The electric force per unit positive test charge at that point: \(\vec{E} = \vec{F}/q_0\)
The product of the source charge and the test charge
The magnetic force per unit charge at that point

question_text: The SI unit of the electric field vector \(\vec{E}\) is:
explanation: The SI unit of the electric field is Newton per Coulomb (N/C), which is dimensionally equivalent to Volt per metre (V/m). It comes directly from \(E = F/q_0\).

question_text: For a point charge \(q\) at distance \(r\), the magnitude of the electric field is:
explanation: The electric field due to a single point charge is \(E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{|q|}{r^2}\). Note it contains only the source charge \(q\), not two charges — that would be the Coulomb force formula.

question_text: Which of the following statements about the electric field is NOT correct?
explanation: Statement D is FALSE. The electric field \(\vec{E}\) is in the same direction as the force on a POSITIVE test charge. For a negative test charge, the force is in the OPPOSITE direction to \(\vec{E}\) since \(\vec{F} = q_0\vec{E}\) and \(q_0 < 0\).

options.text: Electric field is a vector quantity
The electric field does not depend on the test charge
The electric field at a point decreases with increasing distance from the source charge
The electric field is in the same direction as the force on a negative test charge

question_text: The direction of the electric field \(\vec{E}\) at a point is:
explanation: By definition, the direction of \(\vec{E}\) at a point is the direction of the electric force that would be experienced by a small positive test charge placed at that point.

options.text: The direction of force on a negative test charge placed at that point
The direction of force on a positive test charge placed at that point
Perpendicular to the direction of force on any test charge
Always directed toward the nearest conductor

question_text: The electric field always points ________ from a positive source charge and ________ a negative source charge.
explanation: Field lines originate from (point away from) positive charges and terminate at (point towards) negative charges. This is consistent with the force a positive test charge would experience near each type of source charge.

question_text: An electric field cannot exert a net force on:
explanation: A fundamental principle: an electric field cannot exert a net force on the charge that created it. The force a charged body experiences is due to the fields created by OTHER charges.

options.text: A negative charge in the field
A positive test charge in the field
An electric dipole in the field

question_text: Which of these statements about the electric field is FALSE?
explanation: Statement A is false. The SOURCE charge creates the electric field; the TEST charge is used to probe or measure that field. The test charge must be small enough not to disturb the source field.

options.text: The test charge creates the electric field
The source charge creates the electric field
The test charge is the charge on which the electric force is exerted
The electric field at a point is independent of the test charge

question_text: A charge of \(1 \times 10^{-5}\) C experiences a force of 40 N at a certain point. The magnitude of the electric field at that point is:
The electric field at a point 2.0 m from a charge of \(4 \times 10^{-9}\) C is: (\(k = 9 \times 10^9\) N·m²/C²)
What is the magnitude of a point charge whose electric field is 2.0 N/C at a distance of 50 cm? (\(k = 9 \times 10^9\) N·m²/C²)
explanation: Rearranging \(E = k|q|/r^2\): \(q = Er^2/k = (2.0 \times 0.25)/(9\times10^9) = 0.5/(9\times10^9) \approx 5.56 \times 10^{-11}\) C.

question_text: A force of 2.1 N acts on a \(9.2 \times 10^{-4}\) C test charge pushing it westward. The electric field at that point is:
explanation: \(E = F/q_0 = 2.1/(9.2 \times 10^{-4}) \approx 2.28 \times 10^3\) N/C. Since the test charge is positive and pushed westward, \(\vec{E}\) also points westward (same direction as force on positive charge).

question_text: A point charge \(q = -8\) nC is at the origin. The magnitude of the electric field at point P(1.2, -1.6) m is: (\(k = 9 \times 10^9\) N·m²/C²)
The angle that the electric field in Example 2.5 (\(q = -8\) nC at origin, P at (1.2, -1.6) m) makes with the positive x-axis is approximately:
explanation: The field points toward the negative charge (at origin) from P(1.2, -1.6). \(\tan\theta = 1.6/1.2 \Rightarrow \theta_{ref} = 53°\). Since the field points toward the negative charge (into the third quadrant from P's perspective), the angle with the positive x-axis is \(360° - 53° = 307°\) or equivalently \(-53°\).

question_text: The force on an electron (charge \(e = -1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C) in a uniform electric field of \(1 \times 10^4\) N/C has magnitude:
explanation: \(|F| = |q|E = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1 \times 10^4 = 1.6 \times 10^{-15}\) N. The force is opposite to \(\vec{E}\) since the electron is negatively charged.

question_text: The acceleration of an electron (mass \(m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\) kg) in a field of \(1 \times 10^4\) N/C is approximately:
explanation: \(a = F/m = (1.6\times10^{-15})/(9.11\times10^{-31}) \approx 1.76 \times 10^{15}\) m/s². This enormous acceleration reflects the tiny mass of the electron.

question_text: For an electron initially at rest in a field of \(10^4\) N/C, after travelling 1.0 cm, its speed is approximately:
explanation: Using \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as = 0 + 2(1.76\times10^{15})(0.01) = 3.52\times10^{13}\), so \(v = \sqrt{3.52\times10^{13}} \approx 5.9\times10^6\) m/s. (Note the textbook value may vary based on the exact acceleration used.)

question_text: The principle of superposition of electric fields states that the total electric field at any point is:
explanation: Superposition: \(\vec{E}_{total} = \vec{E}_1 + \vec{E}_2 + \vec{E}_3 + \cdots\). The total field is the VECTOR sum, meaning both magnitude and direction of each contribution must be considered.

options.text: The average of the fields due to each individual charge
Equal to the field of the strongest charge only
The vector sum of the fields due to each individual charge
The scalar (algebraic) sum of the magnitudes of all fields

question_text: Two point charges \(q_1 = 12\) nC and \(q_2 = -12\) nC are 10 cm apart. The electric field \(E_1\) at point P (6 cm from \(q_1\), 4 cm from \(q_2\)) due to \(q_1\) is: (\(k = 9\times10^9\) N·m²/C²)
In the same problem (\(q_1 = 12\) nC, \(q_2 = -12\) nC, 10 cm apart), the field \(E_2\) at P (4 cm from \(q_2\)) due to \(q_2\) is: (\(k = 9\times10^9\) N·m²/C²)
In the superposition example above, since both fields at P point in the same direction (toward \(q_2\)), the resultant field \(E_P\) is:
explanation: Since both \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) point in the same direction (from \(q_1\) toward \(q_2\)): \(E_P = E_1 + E_2 = 3.0\times10^4 + 6.8\times10^4 = 9.8\times10^4\) N/C toward \(q_2\).

question_text: Electric field lines are best described as:
explanation: Electric field lines are IMAGINARY lines (visual tools) drawn such that the tangent at any point gives the direction of the electric field \(\vec{E}\) at that point. They also show the path a free positive test charge would follow.

options.text: Real, visible lines of force between charges
Lines of equal potential in the field
Imaginary lines whose tangent at any point gives the direction of \(\vec{E}\)
Lines connecting charges of equal magnitude

question_text: Which of the following is NOT a correct property of electric field lines?
explanation: Electric field lines NEVER cross or intersect each other. If they did, the field at the crossing point would have two different directions simultaneously, which is physically impossible. At every point, \(\vec{E}\) has one unique direction.

options.text: They show the direction of the electric field at each point
Closer lines indicate a stronger electric field
They can cross another line of force in a region of intense electric field
They start on positive charges and end on negative charges

question_text: Why do electric field lines never intersect each other?
explanation: Field lines do not intersect because at any given point, the electric field \(\vec{E}\) has one and only one unique direction. Two crossing lines would imply two different field directions at the same point — a physical impossibility.

options.text: Because electric field is a scalar quantity with no direction
Because at any point, the electric field has only one unique direction
Because field lines can only exist near conductors
Because field lines always travel in straight lines

question_text: The spacing of electric field lines in a region tells us about:
explanation: The density (spacing) of field lines is a visual measure of the field's magnitude. Denser (closer together) lines → stronger field. More spread out (further apart) lines → weaker field.

options.text: The sign of the enclosed charge
The magnitude of the electric field — closer lines mean stronger field
The type of material in that region
The direction of electric current flow

question_text: In a uniform electric field, the field lines are:
explanation: A uniform electric field has constant magnitude and direction everywhere, so its field lines are straight, parallel, and equally spaced — as seen between two large oppositely charged parallel plates.

question_text: An electric dipole consists of:
explanation: An electric dipole is a system of two charges with equal magnitude \(q\) but opposite signs (+q and -q) separated by a small distance \(d\). Together they form a dipole with dipole moment \(P = qd\).

options.text: Two identical positive charges separated by a distance
A single charge surrounded by imaginary field lines
Two charges of equal magnitude but opposite sign separated by a small distance
Two neutral bodies separated by a dielectric

question_text: The net force on an electric dipole placed in a uniform electric field is:
explanation: In a uniform field, the forces on \(+q\) and \(-q\) are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction, so they cancel. The NET FORCE is zero. However, these forces form a couple producing a non-zero torque.

question_text: The torque \(\tau\) exerted on an electric dipole in a uniform field \(E\) at angle \(\theta\) to the dipole axis is:
explanation: The torque on a dipole is \(\tau = qEd\sin\theta = PE\sin\theta\), where \(P = qd\) is the dipole moment. It is maximum at \(\theta = 90°\) and zero when the dipole aligns (\(\theta = 0°\)) or anti-aligns (\(\theta = 180°\)) with the field.

question_text: The electric dipole moment \(P\) is defined as:
explanation: The electric dipole moment is \(P = qd\), the product of each charge's magnitude \(q\) and the separation \(d\) between them. SI unit: Coulomb-metre (C·m). It is a vector pointing from the negative to the positive charge.

question_text: The SI unit of the electric dipole moment is:
explanation: From \(P = qd\): units are Coulombs × metres = C·m (Coulomb-metre). This is also written as C·m in SI.

question_text: The direction of the electric dipole moment vector \(\vec{P}\) is:
explanation: By convention, the dipole moment vector \(\vec{P}\) points from the negative charge (−q) to the positive charge (+q) along the dipole axis.

options.text: From the positive charge to the negative charge
From the negative charge to the positive charge
In the direction of the external electric field

question_text: The potential energy \(U\) of an electric dipole in a uniform electric field is given by:
explanation: The potential energy of a dipole is \(U = -PE\cos\theta = -\vec{P} \cdot \vec{E}\). It is minimum (most stable) when \(\theta = 0°\) (dipole aligned with field) and maximum at \(\theta = 180°\).

question_text: The work done by the electric field when a dipole rotates from orientation \(\theta_i\) to \(\theta_f\) is:
explanation: The work done equals the negative change in potential energy: \(W = U_i - U_f = -(U_f - U_i) = -\Delta U\). A dipole spontaneously rotates to reduce its potential energy.

question_text: A dipole has charges \(\pm 16 \times 10^{-9}\) C and dipole moment \(6.2 \times 10^{-30}\) C·m. The separation between the charges is:
For the same dipole (\(P = 6.2 \times 10^{-30}\) C·m) in a field \(E = 1.5 \times 10^4\) N/C at \(\theta = 145°\), the torque is approximately:
explanation: \(\tau = PE\sin\theta = 6.2\times10^{-30} \times 1.5\times10^4 \times \sin(145°) = 9.3\times10^{-26} \times 0.5736 \approx 5.33\times10^{-26}\) N·m.

question_text: The potential energy of the same dipole (\(P = 6.2 \times 10^{-30}\) C·m, \(E = 1.5 \times 10^4\) N/C, \(\theta = 145°\)) is approximately:
explanation: \(U = -PE\cos\theta = -(6.2\times10^{-30})(1.5\times10^4)\cos(145°) = -(9.3\times10^{-26})(-0.8192) \approx +7.62\times10^{-26}\) J. Positive energy means the dipole is NOT at equilibrium.

question_text: Linear charge density (\(\lambda\)) is defined as:
explanation: Linear charge density \(\lambda = Q/L\) is the charge per unit length. Its SI unit is C/m (Coulombs per metre). It applies when charge is distributed along a line or wire.

options.text: Charge per unit area: \(\sigma = Q/A\), SI unit C/m²
Charge per unit volume: \(\rho = Q/V\), SI unit C/m³
Charge per unit length: \(\lambda = Q/L\), SI unit C/m
Charge per unit time, SI unit C/s

question_text: Surface charge density (\(\sigma\)) is defined as:
explanation: Surface charge density \(\sigma = Q/A\) is the charge per unit area. Its SI unit is C/m² (Coulombs per square metre). It applies when charge is distributed over a 2D surface.

options.text: Charge per unit length: \(\lambda = Q/L\), SI unit C/m
Charge per unit area: \(\sigma = Q/A\), SI unit C/m²
Charge per unit volume: \(\rho = Q/V\), SI unit C/m³
Charge per unit mass, SI unit C/kg

question_text: The SI unit of volume charge density is:
explanation: Volume charge density \(\rho = Q/V\) has SI unit C/m³ (Coulombs per cubic metre). It applies when charge is distributed throughout a 3D volume.

question_text: Charge per unit area is called:
explanation: Charge per unit area (Q/A) is called SURFACE charge density, denoted \(\sigma\), with SI unit C/m².

question_text: The electric field at perpendicular distance \(r\) from an infinite line of charge with linear charge density \(\lambda\) is:
explanation: For an infinite line charge: \(E = \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0 r)\). Note it falls off as \(1/r\) (not \(1/r^2\) as for a point charge) because the line extends infinitely in both directions.

question_text: The electric field due to an infinite line charge decreases with distance \(r\) as:
explanation: From \(E = \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0 r)\), the field is proportional to \(1/r\) — it decreases inversely with distance. This is slower than the \(1/r^2\) fall-off of a point charge.

question_text: Which of the following is NOT a correct unit for the electric field vector?
explanation: V·m (Volt-metre) is NOT a unit of electric field — it is a unit of electric flux. Valid units of electric field are N/C and V/m (equivalent). V·m has the wrong dimensions for a field.

question_text: Newton per Coulomb (N/C) is the SI unit of:
explanation: N/C (Newton per Coulomb) is the SI unit of the electric field vector \(\vec{E}\). It comes directly from the definition \(E = F/q_0\), with force in N and charge in C. It is equivalent to V/m.

question_text: Two point charges \(q_1 = -10\) nC and \(q_2 = -30\) nC are 0.2 m apart. The electric field at the midpoint P is: (\(k = 9\times10^9\) N·m²/C²)
explanation: At midpoint (0.1 m from each): \(E_1 = k\times10\times10^{-9}/(0.1)^2 = 9000\) N/C (toward \(q_1\), leftward); \(E_2 = k\times30\times10^{-9}/(0.1)^2 = 27000\) N/C (toward \(q_2\), rightward). Net: \(27000 - 9000 = 18000 = 1.8\times10^4\) N/C toward \(q_2\).

question_text: How does the electric field of a point charge vary with distance?
explanation: The field of a point charge follows \(E = kq/r^2 \propto 1/r^2\). Doubling the distance reduces the field to one-quarter; tripling reduces it to one-ninth. This is the inverse square law.

options.text: It is constant at all distances
It decreases as the square of the distance (inverse square law)

question_text: The electric field at a point 3.0 cm from an infinite line charge of density \(18.0\,\mu\text{C/m}\) in a medium of relative permittivity 1.5 is approximately: (\(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}\) C²/N·m²)
explanation: \(E = \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_r\varepsilon_0 r) = (18\times10^{-6})/(2\pi\times1.5\times8.85\times10^{-12}\times0.03) \approx 7.19\times10^8\) N/C.

question_text: The electric field produced by a uniformly charged disc depends primarily on:
explanation: For a uniformly charged disc, the electric field on its axis is proportional to the surface charge density \(\sigma\): \(E \propto \sigma\). The more charge per unit area, the stronger the resulting field.
